newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Up to 500,000 refugees trek away from Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Up to 500,000 refugees trek away from Rwanda.

text.p: A stream of up to nearly half a million Rwandan and Burundian refugees were trekking away from Tanzania's border with Rwanda on Friday in a nightmare for aid agencies.
"The situation today is the exodus is still continuing. One thousand people an hour are moving through Kitali (camp)," said Anne Willem Bijleveld of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
Tanzanian troops and police set up a roadblock near another camp, at Lumasi, turning back up to 50,000 refugees, a U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) official said.
Kitali is the camp farthest southeast so the human stream passed through it as it snaked southeast away from Rwanda.

"It's sad, just sad," said Bijleveld, blaming extremist Hutu intimidators for the exodus, which tore into tatters plans by UNHCR and Tanzanian authorities for all 540,000 Rwandan refugees to return home by the end of this month.
"This is all pure manipulation and this is what is the tragedy, a pure humanitarian tragedy," the UNHCR official said.
All seven camps in Benaco region of Ngara had already been emptied or were in the process of emptying, Bijleveld said.

They had more than 494,000 residents between them, including at least 59,000 Burundians, before the exodus started on Sunday. The biggest two were Benaco with 162,000 refugees and Lumasi with 113,000.

The WFP official said Tanzanian troops and police established the roadblock about four km (2.5 miles) southeast of Lumasi camp, cutting off the tail end of a stream of refugees leaving since Thursday.
"There was some chaos while the refugees decided what to do but there were no signs of shots being fired or resistance," she said. "The refugees just turned around and headed north."
"Clearly the majority had already passed and it was a last ditch attempt but they stopped the last 40,000 to 50,000, who headed back towards the Benaco (region) camps," she added.

Members of the Rwandan Hutu militia, the Interahamwe, do not want to go home for fear of prosecution or reprisals for the genocide of up to a million Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994. They want the refugees with them on the grounds of strength in numbers.
Refugees said they left because they believed they would be expelled by Tanzanian authorities back to Rwanda despite some Tanzanian officials saying the repatriation would be voluntary.

The WFP official at Lumasi quoted many refugees as saying they still did not know where they were going but just joined the lines southeast. Some said they were heading to Kenya or Malawi and their leaders would decide exactly where on Friday.
Ngara is about 600 km (370 miles) west of the Kenyan border and 850 km (530 miles) northwest of the Malawi border.

"We (UNHCR) have no credibility in their eyes. We are the ones sending them to Rwanda," said Bijleveld, adding it appeared some Interahamwe recently returned to Rwanda and then come back to the Tanzania camps and said all returnees were being killed.

"They (the intimidators) fooled us incredibly. I think their leadership in Nairobi has a lot to do with this. It's too well organised," said Bijleveld, who was in charge of the operation to send all refugees home from Tanzania by the end of December.
Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, appealed to Tanzanian authorities on Thursday to redirect the refugees back towards their camps without using force.
Near Lumasi camp, aid workers merely watched as a column of refugees who left on Thursday got to their feet at dawn on Friday, loaded belongings on their heads and resumed walking.
"They rested for a few hours during the night and now appear heading towards Barigi game reserve, which has lots of wildlife so they can get food," the WFP official said.

"The reserve is flat but very marshy so our main fear is groups of refugees will break up and scatter so we are looking at a similar situation to eastern Zaire where we lost track of them," she added.

Up to half a million Hutu Rwandan refugees may still be adrift in the equatorial forests of eastern Zaire, where a revolt by Tutsi Zaireans drove more than 500,000 other refugees back into Rwanda last month.
